newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo govt to discuss frozen savings law this week.
newsitem.headline: Yugo govt to discuss frozen savings law this week.

text.p: The Yugoslav government will discuss later this week a bill to release more than $4 billion of private hard currency savings which have been frozen in state banks since 1991, a government source said on Monday.
If approved by the government, the bill will be sent to the federal parliament for adoption, probably by mid-June, said the source, who asked not to be named.

"We are working on this draft very intensively looking at experiences of other republics of former Yugoslavia where those savings were recognized as public debt," a member of an expert team working on the document said.
The expert said the team had urged the government to activate massive immobilised funds during the forthcoming privatisation process in Serbia.
But the new draft privatisation law states that frozen savings can be activated for purchasing shares from the Serbian Share Fund only in the second stage of privatisation.
Economists, holders of frozen savings and opposition political parties are critical of the bill because it excludes depositors from participating in the first wave.
Some experts have proposed that 25 percent of privatisation receipts be directed to a special fund to repay frozen savings.
The draft is now being fine-tuned and the ruling Socialist Party is expected to give its final decision within two weeks.
"This is a purely political decision and we are here to tell the government what its financial resources are. But once the law is adopted there must be no delay in paying back," one expert said.

With state coffers empty and foreign exchange reserves depleted after nearly four years of economic sanctions, the government may find the release of frozen savings a tricky business, economists said.
Economists have suggested that the government compensates savers through a debt-for-equity swap, giving them a stake in privatised companies.
"We work very closely with (the Serbian) privatisation ministry and think that privatisation must primarily focus on holders of frozen savings," the expert said.
But other financial experts disagreed.
"The government should deal with frozen savings in a way appropriate for a public debt. The state must issue bonds to service this debt," a government economist said.
One expert said the government should put debt to citizens on an equal footing with external debt.

"Liabilities to citizens are no less important than those to the outside world. In both cases the debt must be rescheduled," Stojan Dabic, head of the Financial Market Development Centre, told an economist meeting.
But Dabic stressed the debt to Yugoslavs had to be tackled in a slightly different manner.
"The state should take a credit from a foreign financial institution which will issue bonds maturing in 10, 15 or 20 years, with the Yugoslav government repaying on maturity.
"In practice, Yugoslavs would be given bonds denominated in a hard currency and they could sell or use those bonds as collateral in some credit arrangements," Dabic said.
The government expert group, revived after the Yugoslav and the Serbian governments reshuffled earlier this year, made no comment on the issue.
